value.overview: The Green Kingfisher (Chloroceryle americana) is a small tropical kingfisher found from southern Texas through Central and South America to northern Argentina. It is closely associated with freshwater, especially quiet streams, forested rivers, ponds, lagoons, and mangrove channels. The species usually hunts from a low perch above water, diving suddenly to seize prey. Unlike many brightly colored kingfishers, it has a compact shape and mostly green plumage, with noticeable differences between males and females.
value.classification: The Green Kingfisher belongs to the kingfisher family Alcedinidae and the water kingfisher subfamily Cerylinae. It is one of several American kingfishers in the genus Chloroceryle.
value.identification: This is a small, short-tailed kingfisher with a long, straight bill, dark green upperparts, and white spotting on the wings and back. Both sexes have a white throat and collar, while the male has a chestnut breast band and belly markings. Females generally show a green breast band. Juveniles are duller and less strongly marked. In flight, its compact body, rapid wingbeats, and pointed bill are distinctive. It often sits quietly on low branches near water.
value.rangeHabitat: The Green Kingfisher ranges from southern Texas and Mexico through Central America and much of South America to central Argentina. In Costa Rica it is a native resident and breeding species, occurring in suitable lowland and foothill habitats across much of the country, including the Caribbean and Pacific regions. It favors slow-moving or quiet freshwater, forest streams, river edges, ponds, wetlands, and mangrove-lined waterways, usually where overhanging vegetation provides perches and exposed banks provide nesting sites.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident throughout its range. In Costa Rica, it is present year-round and is not considered a regular long-distance migrant, although local movements may follow water conditions, food availability, or seasonal changes in stream flow.
value.breeding: Pairs excavate a nesting tunnel in a vertical or steep earthen bank, usually beside a stream or other water body. The tunnel ends in a nest chamber where the eggs are laid without a substantial nest lining. Both adults participate in excavation, incubation, and feeding the young. Breeding timing varies across the broad range and may be influenced by rainfall and local water conditions. In Costa Rica, breeding occurs in suitable riverine and wetland habitat.
value.dietFeeding: The main food is small fish, which are captured by plunging from a perch into shallow water. The Green Kingfisher also eats aquatic insects, crustaceans such as small shrimp, and occasionally frogs or other small aquatic animals. It commonly hunts from low branches, roots, stones, or human-made structures close to the water. After catching prey, it returns to a perch and swallows smaller items whole.
value.behavior: This kingfisher is usually solitary or found in pairs and spends long periods sitting motionless while watching the water. It makes a rapid, direct dive when prey is detected, then returns to a perch to consume the catch. It can be inconspicuous because of its quiet, patient hunting style and dark green plumage. Calls include sharp, high-pitched notes, especially around territories or during interactions between mates.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered threatened with extinction.
